question: Content growth (a level, an object, a background band) currently bricks the build because the assembler places sections against a frozen table of addresses, and the tool that would refresh that table runs the same placement that just failed. You said get away from this now. Which shape do you want?

options.name: Refresh the frozen table once, with a real band present
options.what: I regenerate the table from a build that has one background band in it, and the frozen mechanism stays. The band builds today.
options.costs: The next time any section grows past its slot, the build bricks again and someone repeats this by hand. It fits exactly one band geometry; the next scene aurora authors can break it.

options.name: Derive placement from order and size; keep the table as an after-the-fact check (Recommended)
options.what: The build places sections from the map's declared order and their real sizes. The hardware-fixed addresses (DAC banks at 0x0/0x10000/0x48000, the bank bases) stay fixed; everything else floats. The frozen table becomes an expectation the test suite checks against, and a moved boundary prints a warning naming the section and the delta instead of failing the build. The engine lane keeps its byte-attribution tooling. First step is small (one file), byte-neutral while nothing has grown, and lets one band build without moving anything by hand.
options.costs: A couple of days across my lane and the engine lane: my parcel, then one refreeze through the engine lane. The engine's ceiling-printing script must be re-pointed. Sections that grow now move their neighbours silently-but-loudly (a warning, not a failure), so a byte-change you did not expect shows up as a warning line rather than a red build — you have to read the warning.

options.name: Delete the frozen tables outright
options.what: Same derived placement, but no committed table at all; the only frozen thing left is the ROM checksum where a shape is meant to be identical.
options.costs: The test suite loses the oracle that tells you WHICH section moved when a checksum changes; you find out by diffing. It also re-opens a code-size relaxation edge the tables currently guard. Buys nothing the checksum chain does not already prove.

recommend.because: The code is already most of the way there — order is map-driven and non-anchored sections already pack — so this removes the last three places the table decides bytes rather than redesigning placement. It is the only option that both builds today's band AND stops the next one from bricking the build, while keeping the loud-not-silent property the engine lane asked for. One warning to read beats a red build nobody can regenerate.

question: A struct in the game's source often ends with a filler field whose size someone worked out by hand. When a field above it changes, that number is silently wrong. I have drafted a way to let the author say where the next field should start and have the compiler work the filler out. Do you want it, and in which shape?

options.name: Both forms, plus a nudge when the risky one is used (Recommended)
options.what: Two ways to write filler: say where the next field starts and the compiler sizes it (the safe one), or say how many spare bytes you are reserving (the honest use of the second one — reserved space, where the count is the real intention). When someone writes the second in a place where the first was clearly meant, the build says so and prints the exact line to write instead.
options.costs: Two things to learn instead of one, and a new warning that could be wrong occasionally. The engine lane asked for only the first form and would be half-overruled here.

options.name: Only the safe form
options.what: One way to write filler: say where the next field starts. Nothing else is added to the language.
options.costs: Reserving a block of spare bytes — where the count IS the thing you mean, and the offset is what moves — has to be written by naming an offset you did not care about. The language already uses the other word elsewhere for exactly this, so refusing it here means the same word means different things in two places.

options.name: Not now
options.what: Leave it. The alignment check I shipped last week still catches a stale filler loudly; someone just has to fix the number by hand each time.
options.costs: The engine lane keeps hand-counting, and the one live case stays wrong-by-name (the field is called after the offset 93 and actually sits at 118).

recommend.because: The safe form is what the engine lane needs and it is in every option. The disagreement is only about whether to also keep the plain 'reserve N bytes' spelling: refusing it does not remove the hazard, because someone reserving spare bytes then has to write an offset they do not mean, and the word already means exactly that elsewhere in the language. A warning that names the mistake and prints the fix does more than removing the word would.

question: When engine source embeds a data file, the path is read from the project root - except one file, which writes its path relative to itself and works only because a single line in my tool names that file specifically. options.what: Relative-to-the-file becomes a genuine, supported way to write these paths, available everywhere rather than to one named file.
options.costs: Real implementation work in the compiler, a new rule authors must learn, and two ways to spell the same thing forever. Buys convenience for files that sit deep in a directory tree.

options.what: Change nothing.
options.costs: The current state teaches every reader that relative paths work, when they work for exactly one hardcoded filename. The next person to copy that style gets a build failure and no clue why - and the line looks like a considered exception rather than the leftover it is.

That folder is gitignored, so git shows nothing and nobody can tell it happened. Should an unset setting refuse by name instead of quietly using your working folder?

options.name: Refuse by name when nobody says where the tree is
options.what: Running the tests without setting the location stops immediately with an error naming what is missing, instead of silently working against your live folder. The mistake becomes loud and local, and is fixed in a minute.
options.costs: Anyone running the suite bare, without setting the variable, now gets a refusal where they used to get a run. Every lane has to be told before it moves. options.costs: A wrong or unset location can never announce itself. Your build regenerates those files anyway so nothing gets corrupted - but anything that READS them without rebuilding first gets whatever last wrote them, and no record anywhere says who did. Measured: one two-test run rewrote all nineteen files in your tree while git status stayed completely clean.

recommend.because: The argument is invisibility, not damage. The engine lane checked and their build regenerates all nineteen files unconditionally, so it is self-healing against a foreign write - I am deliberately NOT selling this as a corruption risk, because that framing is scarier, testable, and would lose. What survives is that a silent fallback to somebody's live working folder is structurally incapable of announcing its own failure, and the gitignore removes the last place a person could notice. Both lanes that measured it recommend the same.

answered.did: Implementing the narrow scope first - the 29 write-reaching call sites, not all 127 - so the loud half is closed without changing behaviour for every lane at once. Reversible on read-back; if the owner disagrees the change is one revert.

question: When a repeat block's count is a number the assembler has not worked out yet - the count sits above the label that defines it - the size of the block depends on the number and the number depends on the size of the block. Sigil currently tries sixteen times and then says 'did not converge within 16 passes'. What should it say instead? This is the exact complaint the Sonic community makes about AS, so answering it with a bigger number would be adopting the thing we are trying to replace.

options.what: Tell the author it is circular, by name. Detect that the count cannot be settled because it depends on its own block, and refuse with a message naming the label, the repeat, and the loop between them.
options.costs: Some programs AS happens to get away with would now be refused, so a real disassembly might need a source edit. But the refusal is instant and says exactly what to change.

options.what: Keep trying, and report honestly when it fails. Same as today but the message names which symbols were still moving and what they moved between, instead of quoting a pass count.
options.costs: Accepts more existing code, but the answer to a genuinely circular program is still 'it did not settle', which is the answer people dislike. The sixteen is still there, just no longer printed.

options.what: Both, split by which it actually is. Refuse the provably circular case by name; for everything else keep settling with no fixed number of attempts, and only if it truly oscillates report the moving symbols.
options.costs: The most work of the three, and the detection has to be right - calling something circular when it merely needed one more attempt would refuse a valid program.

recommend: Both, split by which it actually is
because: The two situations are different and today we give them the same answer. 'This cannot be worked out, here is the loop' is a real answer an author can act on; 'I tried sixteen times' is not an answer at all, it is a description of our own effort. Splitting them is the whole difference between Sigil and the assembler we are replacing, and a magic number in an error message is the thing the community named when asked what they hate.

question: In our own language, a label is a name pointing at a place in the game's code. There is a way to say "no label here" - you write 0 - and we already blessed that spelling for comparisons. But if you try to give 0 to a function expecting a label, it refuses. Meanwhile a function can DECLARE 0 as its own fallback for such a slot and nobody checks it, so the spelling reads as legal, gets written down, and only fails when someone actually calls it. Aeon prescribed that exact spelling in ten places - a generated banner, the generator behind it, a gate's own error message, a contract row, two to-do items and a test fixture - and not one had ever been run. Should 0 be accepted as "no label" everywhere, or refused everywhere?

options.what: 0 becomes a legal way to say "no label" wherever a label is expected. All ten of aeon's places become correct without anyone editing them, and the language says the same thing in every position.
options.costs: We are making 0 permanently mean "nothing" for labels. That is close to unremovable once the game is written using it - though we already committed to it for comparisons, so this is finishing a decision rather than starting one.

options.what: Writing 0 as a label's fallback becomes an error at the point someone writes it, so the misleading spelling cannot be recorded at all.
options.costs: Eleven places already written down become errors and have to be rewritten, including one in the shared contract repo that is not ours. And it takes away the workaround aeon is currently relying on.

options.what: Leave it. Aeon has a spelling that builds, so nothing is blocked today.
options.costs: The misleading shape stays: it reads usable, is not, and the next person writes the same ten sites. This already happened once.

recommend.because: It is not really a new decision. We already ruled that 0 means "no label" when comparing - it is written into our own guidance as the empty-slot spelling. So the language already says this in one place and refuses it in another, and the refusal is the inconsistent half rather than the safe one. It also costs nobody any rewriting. Worth knowing: there is a related hole on our side where the check is silently skipped for lists of labels, which is why aeon had a GREEN example sitting two lines from the broken one, teaching everyone the wrong lesson. That hole is mine to close and I cannot close it until you answer, because closing it the other way would turn aeon's working code red.
